stemBlocks.value: Think first: Two fractions with different denominators must be rewritten over one common denominator before they can be subtracted.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p050-q03 from workbook page 50.

solutionSteps.instruction: Write the common denominator as the product of the two denominators.
Rewrite each fraction over that denominator.

contentBlocks.value: 9 is multiplied by (x − 2); 4 is multiplied by (x + 5)

solutionSteps.instruction: Expand both brackets in the numerator.

strategyBlocks.value: Use (x + 5)(x − 2) as the common denominator, adjust each numerator accordingly, then expand and collect like terms.

whyThisWorks.value: Fractions can only be combined when they measure the same sized pieces, and multiplying each fraction by a well-chosen form of 1 changes its appearance without changing its value. Here 9/(x + 5) becomes 9(x − 2)/[(x + 5)(x − 2)], which is the same number written over the shared denominator. Once both pieces are the same size, subtraction acts on the numerators alone.

commonErrors.misconception: Subtracting only the first term of the second numerator, giving 9x − 18 − 4x + 20.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Subtracting only the first term of the second numerator, giving 9x − 18 − 4x + 20.

commonErrors.misconception: Adding the denominators instead of multiplying them.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Adding the denominators instead of multiplying them.

commonErrors.misconception: Expanding the denominator unnecessarily, which makes the answer harder to read and to check.

examTip.value: Put the second numerator in brackets before you subtract. Writing −(4x + 20) rather than −4x + 20 stops the most common sign slip in this whole topic.
